lesson.title: 4G LTE: When Cellular Networks Went All-IP
lesson.summary: 4G LTE is the cellular technology generation that rebuilt mobile networks around an all-IP data architecture and efficient spectrum sharing techniques, delivering the fast mobile broadband speeds that made streaming video and app-based smartphones practical.
lesson.body:
Earlier cellular generations were built primarily around carrying voice calls, with data added on top of a network designed for circuit-switched telephone connections. As smartphones and mobile data use exploded, that architecture became a poor fit: streaming video, app downloads, and constant background data traffic need a network genuinely designed for data from the ground up, not one adapting a voice-first design. LTE, Long Term Evolution, was the industry's answer, a redesign of the cellular network's core, still built on the cells and frequency reuse from the cellular network concept, but rebuilt end to end for IP data.

It is worth being precise here, because the marketing and the technical standards do not perfectly line up. LTE is a 3GPP technical standard, and 4G is a generational marketing label; early LTE deployments were marketed as 4G before they technically met the full data rate requirements the ITU had set for true fourth generation service, and it was really LTE-Advanced, a later enhancement, that formally satisfied those requirements. In everyday use, though, 4G and LTE are used essentially interchangeably to mean the same generation of mobile network technology.

Architecturally, LTE's core network, called the Evolved Packet Core, is built entirely around IP packet switching rather than the older circuit-switched voice model, meaning voice calls themselves eventually moved to running as IP data too, a service called Voice over LTE, or VoLTE. On the radio side, LTE uses Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access, OFDMA, for the downlink from tower to phone, splitting the available spectrum into many closely spaced narrow subcarriers that can be assigned flexibly to different users based on their signal conditions, and a related technique, Single Carrier FDMA, for the uplink from phone to tower, chosen specifically because it is more power efficient for battery-constrained mobile devices than standard OFDMA would be.

Consider a commuter riding a train who starts streaming a video, browses a map application, and sends a few text messages, all within the same few minutes, all over the same LTE connection. Under the hood, the Evolved Packet Core treats every one of those activities identically, as IP packets flowing to and from the phone, rather than routing the phone call and text messages down one kind of dedicated channel and the video stream down another the way older, voice-centric cellular architectures effectively had to. The tower's OFDMA scheduler is also continuously deciding, many times per second, which subcarriers to hand this particular phone based on its current signal quality and how much data it is requesting, sharing the same finite spectrum fairly across every other phone connected to that same cell at the same time.

Peak theoretical LTE downlink speeds can reach into the hundreds of megabits per second under ideal conditions, though real-world speeds are typically much lower once distance from the tower, obstacles, and the number of other users sharing the same cell are accounted for, the same frequency reuse and shared-cell tradeoffs described in the cellular network concept. LTE, and the 5G networks that have since extended its all-IP, OFDMA-based approach even further, represent the point where cellular networks stopped being phone networks that also carried a bit of data and became genuinely general-purpose mobile internet infrastructure.
